'''Manfred Donike''' (23 August 1933, [[Erftstadt|Köttingen]], [[Rhine Province]] &ndash; 21 August 1995, on a flight from [[Frankfurt am Main]] to [[Johannesburg]]) was a German [[cycle sport|cyclist]] and chemist, known for his research on [[Doping (sport)|doping]].<ref name="SportsRef">{{cite web |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/athletes/do/manfred-donike-1.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417184703/https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/athletes/do/manfred-donike-1.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=17 April 2020 |title=Manfred Donike Olympic Results |accessdate=5 June 2015 |publisher=Sports Reference}}</ref> Donike lived in [[Rölsdorf]].

Donike studied chemistry in [[Cologne]] and graduated in 1965. By 1972, Donike had developed a procedure capable of accurate detection of banned substances and their metabolites through analysis, using [[gas chromatography]] and [[mass spectrometry]], of urine. In 1977, Donike was hired by the [[German Sport University Cologne]] to lead the biochemistry department.

In 1960 and 1961, Donike competed in the [[Tour de France]]. His son, also called [[Manfred Donike (cyclist, born 1960)|Manfred]], competed at the [[1984 Summer Olympics]].<ref name="SportsRef" />

Donike died of a heart attack on 21 August 1995 in an aeroplane while en route to Johannesburg, South Africa.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/08/22/obituaries/manfred-donike-testing-expert-61.html|title=Manfred Donike, Testing Expert, 61|agency=Associated Press|work=The New York Times|page=D20|date=22 August 1995}}</ref>
